- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
### The Repair Table

Every Saturday, a folding table appears outside the library in my neighborhood. It has a blue plastic cloth, a jar of mismatched screwdrivers, and a handwritten sign that says, “BRING YOUR BROKEN THINGS.” At first, I assumed it was a charity collection. Then I noticed a woman in a green coat taking apart a toaster while its owner watched, holding the loose crumb tray like a serving dish.

The table belongs to no shop or organization. It was started by a retired electrician named Luis, who got tired of seeing useful objects left beside the trash bins. He put a notice on the library bulletin board, borrowed the table, and showed up one Saturday with his tools. Three people came. One brought a lamp, one brought a radio, and one brought a cake.

The lamp needed a new plug. The radio could not be saved, though Luis kept it open for an hour, tracing wires with a magnifying glass. The cake, as it happened, needed nothing at all. Its maker had misunderstood the notice and thought the event was a neighborhood party. She stayed anyway, cutting slices with a pocketknife while Luis worked.

A year later, the repair table has a small crowd of regulars. There is Priya, who sews torn coats and replaces buttons. There is Ben, a teenager who can diagnose many computer problems but has not yet learned to arrive on time. There is Mrs. Chen, who specializes in umbrellas and says that most people open them too roughly. Nobody has found a polite way to disagree with her.

I began stopping by because my apartment is on the way to the library, and because watching someone solve a problem is a pleasant form of rest. The work is usually slow. There are screws to sort, parts to inspect, and long pauses while somebody searches for the right word. Sometimes a repairer simply looks at an object from every angle, turning it over in their hands.

One morning, a boy brought in a toy train that had stopped moving. It was bright red, with a smiling face painted on the front, and he placed it on the table with great care. Ben opened the battery compartment and found a spring bent flat. He lifted it gently with a screwdriver, inserted fresh batteries, and set the train on the pavement. It moved about two feet before striking a crack.

The boy cheered. His mother thanked Ben, then asked what she owed him. Ben pointed to the jar beside the sign, which contained a few coins, two safety pins, and an orange button. She put in five dollars. The boy asked if he could have the button, and after some discussion, his mother exchanged it for a coin from her purse.

Not everything ends so neatly. A man once brought a coffee grinder that had belonged to his father. Its motor had burned out, and the replacement part was no longer made. Luis searched online for a while, then explained the problem. The man nodded, but did not take the grinder back immediately. He asked whether the motor might still be useful to someone, even if it would never run again.

Luis said he could keep the cord and the little rubber feet. The rest would probably have to go to an electronics recycling depot. The man considered this, then asked for a screwdriver. He removed the rubber feet himself and put them in his coat pocket. He left the grinder with Luis and walked away carrying only its glass jar, which he said he might use for screws.

The table has changed my sense of what a broken thing is. I used to imagine an object passing abruptly from useful to useless: a switch clicks, nothing happens, and the object becomes trash. At the table, that moment stretches out. A failure might be caused by a dirty contact, a loose wire, or a part that costs less than a bus ticket. Sometimes the cause remains a mystery.

There are practical reasons to be cautious about this way of thinking. Repairs take time, tools, and knowledge. A cheap replacement can cost less than an afternoon of skilled work, and some objects are sealed so tightly that opening them causes further damage. The volunteers do not pretend otherwise. They often tell people to buy a replacement, especially when an electrical item seems unsafe.

Still, they are willing to look first. That willingness draws people who have nowhere else to take a wobbly chair or a jacket with a broken zipper. It also draws people with questions. A woman who came for a lamp repair returned the next week to learn how to replace a plug. She practiced on an old cord, under Luis’s supervision, and took notes on an envelope.

By the time winter arrived, the library offered the group a corner indoors. The volunteers were reluctant to lose their spot by the entrance, where passersby could see them, but the first cold morning settled the matter. They carried the table inside and set it up between the returns desk and a shelf of travel guides. Mrs. Chen brought a small rug to catch the water dripping from umbrellas.

On the last Saturday before the holidays, the table was crowded. Priya worked on a child’s coat while the child sat nearby drawing a map of a kingdom made entirely of stairs. Ben was late, but arrived carrying a box of cables he had sorted by size. Luis had brought a thermos of coffee, and the cake maker appeared again with a tin of cookies. This time she knew what the gathering was.

As I left, I saw the boy with the red train coming through the door. He was older by several inches and carried the train under one arm. I wondered if it had broken again, but he set it on the rug and switched it on. It ran past the legs of the table, slowed at the edge, and stopped. He picked it up, turned it around, and sent it back the other way.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A gently structured literary narrative uses recurring characters and objects to build toward a quiet, open-ended ending.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and patient, finding meaning in small acts of attention rather than dramatic transformation. Its pathos is understated: the man with his father’s broken grinder does not save the object, but takes its rubber feet and glass jar; the boy’s train returns at the end, still moving imperfectly. The reader is invited to see repair as both practical work and a way of staying with things, while the essay resists pretending that every object—or problem—can be fixed.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds broken household objects, improvised tools, neighbors sharing skills, and the slow, social work of deciding what is worth saving. Its moral emphasis is on looking closely before discarding, balanced by a clear acknowledgment of cost, safety, and irreparable failure. The recurring red train makes persistence feel playful rather than triumphant.

## Evidence line
> The table has changed my sense of what a broken thing is.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the recurring repair objects, restrained sentiment, and qualified hope make this a distinctive, coherent sample.
